overview: This file traces U.S. engagement with Japanese newspapers from the immediate end of the Pacific War through the Allied Occupation, linking press policy, propaganda control, democratization, labor relations, circulation, and institutional preservation. Its documents cover the suppression of Japanese propaganda publications in Argentina; the distribution of post-surrender Tokyo newspapers to Japanese communities in Brazil and Peru; the history, ownership, finances, editorial policy, employee movement, and joint-management system of the Yomiuri; British concerns about receiving timely news from occupied Japan; a statistical SCAP study of rural and urban circulation for 113 Japanese daily newspapers; personnel and editorial problems at Pacific Stars and Stripes; and attempts to place a long run of the Mainichi Shimbun in an American research library.
interest: The file is especially useful because it treats newspapers simultaneously as political instruments, commercial institutions, workplaces, and measurable networks of readership. The detailed Yomiuri reports provide an unusually close view of how occupation-era democratization intersected with employee activism, union contracts, ownership, finance, and editorial control, while the study of 113 dailies offers substantial quantitative evidence for comparing rural and urban media penetration across Japan. The South American correspondence also broadens the file’s value beyond occupied Japan by showing U.S. officials attempting first to suppress wartime Japanese influence and then to reshape diaspora opinion through selected post-surrender news. Finally, the proposed sale of the Mainichi archive reveals contemporary decisions about preservation and access that later affected the source base available to historians.
